sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: The orbit a satellite occupies determines what it can see, when, and how often. Remote sensing missions are mostly in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), with a subset in Geosynchronous (GEO). The dominant LEO design for Earth observation is the **Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO)**: a near-polar orbit whose precession exactly compensates for Earth's revolution around the Sun, ensuring the satellite always crosses the equator at the same local solar time.

sections.text: ## Keplerian Orbital Elements

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: Six numbers completely specify an orbit:

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
  a = semi-major axis (size: determines period via Kepler's 3rd law)
  e = eccentricity (shape: 0=circle, 1=parabola)
  i = inclination (tilt relative to equatorial plane)
  RAAN = right ascension of ascending node (longitude of ascending node)
  omega = argument of perigee (where in orbit is closest approach)
  nu = true anomaly (where the satellite is now along the orbit)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
For circular LEO EO missions:
  e ~ 0 (circular orbit)
  a ~ 6778 km (= 6371 km Earth radius + 407 km altitude)
  i ~ 97-99 degrees (retrograde! slightly more than 90 deg for SSO)
```

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
**Kepler's Third Law for circular orbit**:
```
  T^2 = (4*pi^2 / mu) * a^3

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
mu = G * M_Earth = 3.986e14 m^3/s^2
  T = 2*pi * sqrt(a^3 / mu)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
At a = 6778 km:  T = 92.6 minutes (~15 orbits/day)
  At a = 7178 km:  T = 100 minutes (~14.4 orbits/day)
```

sections.text: ## Sun-Synchronous Orbit: The Engineering

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: The Earth is not a perfect sphere -- the equatorial bulge (J2 perturbation) causes orbital plane precession. SSO exploits this:

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
NATURAL PRECESSION (J2 effect)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
For a satellite at inclination i and altitude h:
  dRAAN/dt = -3/2 * (R_E/a)^2 * (J2/T) * cos(i)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: where J2 = 1.08263e-3 (Earth's oblateness coefficient)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
To match Earth's orbital rate around Sun: dRAAN/dt = +360 deg/year
    = +0.9856 deg/day (eastward)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
For prograde orbits (i < 90 deg), precession is westward (-cos).
  Need RETROGRADE orbit (i > 90 deg) to get positive precession.

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Typical SSO parameters:
    h = 705 km, i = 98.2 deg -> precession = +0.986 deg/day  [Landsat]
    h = 786 km, i = 98.6 deg -> precession = +0.986 deg/day  [Sentinel-2]
    h = 693 km, i = 98.2 deg -> precession = +0.986 deg/day  [Sentinel-1]
```

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: The result: the orbital plane maintains a fixed angle relative to the Sun-Earth line. The satellite crosses the equator at the same **Local Solar Time (LST)** on every pass.

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
WHY SAME LOCAL SOLAR TIME MATTERS

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Without SSO:
  Pass 1: 10:30 AM -- shadows point southwest, sun angle 45 deg
  Pass 2 (3 months later): 4:00 PM -- shadows point east, sun angle 30 deg
  -> Images incomparable due to different illumination geometry

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
With SSO (e.g., 10:30 AM descending node):
  Every pass: 10:30 AM local solar time
  Sun angle, shadow length, illumination direction: consistent
  -> Time series analysis is valid
  -> Seasonal changes not confused with illumination changes
```

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: **Descending vs. ascending node**: Most optical EO satellites use a descending (south-going) daytime pass with local solar time ~10-11 AM. Sentinel-1 SAR uses ascending (north-going) pass. The morning (10 AM) time was chosen to minimize cloud cover (clouds tend to build in the afternoon).

sections.text: ## Repeat Cycle and Ground Track Geometry

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: A sun-synchronous satellite does not cover the same ground track every orbit. It has a repeat cycle after which the ground tracks exactly repeat:

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
GROUND TRACK GEOMETRY

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Each orbit advances by delta_lambda (deg) in longitude:
    delta_lambda = 360 / (orbits_per_day) - precession_per_orbit

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
For Landsat 9 (16-day repeat, 233 orbits per cycle):
    Day 1: tracks 1, 18, 35, 52... (every 233rd track spacing)
    Day 2: tracks shifted by 1/16 of total ground width
    Day 16: full coverage achieved

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Landsat WRS-2: 233 paths (north-south strips), each 185km wide
    Adjacent paths overlap at equator: ~7.6 km overlap
    Adjacent paths overlap at 60 deg latitude: ~50%
    Polar regions: maximum overlap

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
SWATH vs SPATIAL RESOLUTION TRADE:
    Wide swath (low GSD): MODIS 2330km, daily global
    Moderate swath (moderate GSD): Landsat 185km, 16-day global
    Narrow swath (high GSD): WorldView-3 13km, 1-4 day (opportunistic)
```

sections.text: ### Revisit Time vs. Resolution: Fundamental Trade-off

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs
Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: The fundamental trade-off exists because a satellite moves at fixed speed (~7.5 km/s). Wider field of view = larger image per pass = more ground covered = faster global repeat. But wider FOV means smaller telescope focal length for the same detector area = coarser GSD. You cannot escape this geometric constraint.

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: **Planet's solution**: launch hundreds of small satellites. 200+ Doves = daily global 3-5m coverage. The trade-off is dodged by adding more platforms, not changing per-satellite physics.

sections.text: ## Geostationary Orbit (GEO)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: At 35,786 km, orbital period = 24 hours exactly. Satellite appears stationary relative to Earth.

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
GEO SATELLITES FOR REMOTE SENSING

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites):
    GOES-West (135.4 W): covers western Americas + Pacific
    GOES-East (75.2 W):  covers eastern Americas + Atlantic
    Sensor: ABI (Advanced Baseline Imager), 16 channels
    Full disk every 15 min, CONUS every 5 min, mesoscale 60 sec

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
ADVANTAGES:
    - Continuous temporal coverage (minutes to seconds)
    - Severe weather monitoring, hurricane tracking
    - Diurnal cycle resolved (watch clouds form and dissipate)
    - No revisit gap -- always staring at same area

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
DISADVANTAGES:
    - Pixel size at nadir: 500m (visible), 2km (thermal)
    - Polar areas poorly observed (high off-nadir angle)
    - Parallax error for clouds at altitude (cloud top vs. bottom different position)
    - High orbit = weak signal -> requires large telescope for same SNR
    - Cannot do InSAR or lidar from GEO (not yet operational)
```

sections.text: ## Orbit Determination and GPS in Orbit

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text: Modern EO satellites carry onboard GPS receivers for precision orbit determination (POD):

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
```
GNSS-based POD for EO satellites

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Onboard GPS receiver: records pseudorange + carrier phase
  Post-processing (ground): precise orbit determination
  Accuracy: 1-5 cm (for InSAR-quality orbits, key for Sentinel-1)

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Sentinel-1 POD specifications:
    Restituted orbit (3h after pass): 5 cm RMS
    Precise orbit (20 days after): 1 cm RMS
    -> Used for InSAR processing where orbit error = phase error

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
Orbit error effect on InSAR:
    1 cm orbit error at 700km altitude -> ~0.5 mm phase error
    For mm-level deformation detection: precise orbits required
```

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Satellite Orbits: Mechanics, Sun-Synchronous, Revisit Trade-offs

sections.text:
| If you need to diagnose... | Start With | Key Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Daily global optical | Low sun-synchronous orbit with wide swath | Wide swath means coarse spatial resolution. |
| Daily 3-5 m optical | LEO SSO constellation | Revisit comes from fleet size, not one satellite. |
| 5-day 10 m optical | Sentinel-2 A+B SSO geometry | Revisit differs from repeat cycle and can be cloud-limited. |
| 16-day archive continuity | Landsat SSO ground track | Cross-sensor calibration matters across decades. |
| Minute-scale weather refresh | Geostationary orbit | GEO sacrifices high-latitude geometry and fine resolution. |
| Sub-meter tasking | Narrow-swath commercial SSO | Tasking priority and off-nadir angle affect data quality. |
| All-weather 6-day radar | Sentinel-1-style SSO C-band SAR | Radar repeat does not guarantee interferometric coherence. |
| L-band 12-day radar | NISAR-style SSO L-band SAR | Longer wavelength helps vegetation but not all decorrelation. |
| Polar cryosphere coverage | Near-polar SSO | Orbit coverage does not imply constant illumination. |
| Continuous ocean/SST | GEO or daily-global LEO | Clouds still limit passive thermal ocean retrieval. |
